Bucky Pizzarelli

Bucky Pizzarelli has played on countless jazz and pop recordings over the years. He was born in Paterson, New Jersey on January 9, 1926 and played guitar and banjo as a youth, often in family jam sessions. A career in music was never in doubt and he joined the Vaughn Monroe Orchestra at age 17. Bucky moved to New York after military service and found work at NBC, ABC and later with The Three Suns Trio. As a “first call” studio player, he recorded with numerous jazz and popular music groups and became the guitarist in the original Tonight Show band. His duo recordings with Stephane Grappelli, Zoot Sims and Bud Freeman are among his favorites and his personal guitar style is welcomed at jazz venues across the country. Bucky’s son John is following in his father’s career and is one of the most popular guitarists/vocalists in today’s jazz scene.
Bucky was interviewed at the Jerome Jazz Party in Aspen, Colorado on October 11, 1997, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

We are filming today in Aspen, Colorado for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and it’s a great pleasure to welcome Bucky Pizzarelli, guitarist extraordinaire. I hate to tell you this but someone sold you a guitar with too many strings.
No I’ve had that for quite a while now you know, thanks to George Van Eps, a seven string, since ‘68, ‘69 I think, that’s when I started with it.
Was it a big adjustment at first?

It was. I was doing a lot of studio work and in the evenings I was doing The Tonight Show. And I went to Manny’s Music Store on 48th Street and bought a seven string Gretsch after I heard George Van Eps play it the night before in a night club. And I think about five or six guitar players in New York City all bought them the same day.
He made a big impression then. Is it always the lower string that’s added — on the seven string?

Well there are variations. Lenny Breau for instance has an extra string, only it’s a high string. And on the six string actually sometimes you tune it down to a D. This is a low A. And I’ve seen some tuned to low B flat.
A B flat?
Yeah.
That seems an odd note to put on the bottom of a guitar.

Yeah. An old friend of mine from Princeton, Bill Priestly, an architect from — a very good architect — from Chicago, had one, a seven string, in 1929, an old Martin, he just put an extra peg up there and put another string on. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
Did you come from a musical family? Because I know your family now is pretty darned musical.

Oh yes. My two uncles taught me how to play and they told me who to listen to, you know, Benny Goodman’s band and George Van Eps and Alan Reuss and Charlie Christian. But they happened to be very good. My older uncle, Peter Domenick, had a day job so he never thought of going on the road but was very capable of playing with any band in those days. He was an expert banjo player. And my younger uncle, Bobby, did go on the road with Bob Chester, Raymond Scott, Buddy Rodgers, dance bands, playing rhythm guitar.
So you were a teenager in the early 40s? You were born in ‘26?
Okay. So you kind of were right in the middle of the swing heyday.

Well I was fortunate because of my uncles guiding me, telling me who to listen to, only by way of radio, and a few 78s of Charlie Christian and maybe Django Reinhardt. But they were always up on whatever they had to play, they happened to play it correctly, which was in my favor, because they passed it on to me to make sure everything — the bass notes were right, the chords were right.
Did you learn to read music also at this time?

A little then. And then as I got into the band business I found out what I really had to know how to do so I jumped on the bandwagon and started to learn what was required. In those days mostly it was rhythm, and a few little solos here and there.
Was Vaughn Monroe your first full time—
Oh yeah. I was just 17, I just got out of high school and I was about to be drafted as soon as I turned 18, you know they were taking them right after 18. You were in the Army in two weeks.
This was right at the tail end of the war, right?
The beginning.
Oh. Okay.

I’m talking about 1943 I went with Vaughan and I turned 18 in ‘44 and because I was on the road with Vaughan a little bit, about three or four months, I wasn’t drafted until April. But I got a touch of the band, and I said that’s for me.
So when you anticipated getting out of the service you knew what you wanted to do.
Oh, Vaughan gave me the job back. I was in the service for two years. I was in Europe at the tail end of the German war and from then I went to the Philippine Islands for nine months.
What was your role in the military? © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
I was a PFC, I did nothing but shoot baskets. We had nothing to do. The war was over. We were sitting around Manila doing nothing.
No kidding. Did you get to play at all?

Oh yeah, we did play a lot. So we listened to a lot of V-discs in those days, all the best records. I heard Nat King Cole on these big records, you know they had these large 15 minute transcriptions, with a big long arm and they would play them and they’d last 15 minutes.
15 minutes. You know now that seems like nothing. It’s like such an annoyance with the LPs now, you have to turn them over.

Oh they were the best records. I mean Vaughn made some V-discs and in fact some of the best music is on those discs today if you can ever find them. But all the great bands made what they call V-discs.
Doing their part for the war effort.
Yeah.
Vaughn Monroe’s music wasn’t considered jazz?

No but he had a jazz flair to it. They played some fast tempos and they had a great arranger there named Johnny Watson who wrote the theme song and he had about 25 originals “Take it Jackson” and all kinds of – “Harvard Square” — I mean originals. I mean just little vehicles for the jazz people to play on.
Almost like Paul Whiteman, they had some hot players mixed in there?

Yeah, well Paul was a little more I would say like symphony kind of thing, they were more classical end. And Vaughn’s band had some good players in it, some real good soloists. We had a great lead alto player, Andy Bagni. The band was built around what he did.
What was the work like at that time? Was it dances?

All dance jobs. And we’d jump on a bus and go, average 200 miles a night, or 250, play in Sioux City, Iowa and the next — you’re in another place. I mean I was single, it didn’t matter to me, I just jumped on the bus and I was happy to be there. It didn’t matter. Those long trips never bothered me.
Could I ask you what you were making at that time?
$125 a week. And we did a radio show which paid $60 on Saturday, it was a national show, the Camel Caravan. So that was a lot of money.
At that time that was pretty good money, right? To do, especially what you liked.
Oh yeah, yeah.
Well after that you know, how do you make it in the jazz world, at that point?

It’s hard today because you can go to college today and get a degree in performance, which we were never offered in those days. But I think the thing that’s wrong about that © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

is that the kids are too over trained so that if they get a job with the Glenn Miller band or the Tommy Dorsey band, they can read those books with their eyes closed after one week. And then boredom sets in if they’re not playing any solos. If that’s what they want to be, so there’s no place. But you know, the Stan Getz, Zoot Sims, and all the great soloists, only played eight measures in those days in the bands. Vido Musso with the “Jersey Bounce” with Benny Goodman, even Artie Shaw and Benny Goodman, solos were not ever 32 measures. And if you were given an eight bar solo, you had to say something in eight measures, which is very difficult. Today, kids play for a half hour. I don’t know what they’re saying.
Well in the early ‘50s then, after you were — how long were you with Monroe?
Oh I left around ‘52, ‘53.
So had you started to establish a reputation or did you have to kind of start from the beginning?

You know what happened, we had, through this radio show we had a violin section just to play the show with us every Saturday. They would complement the six violins that we had, we had another six come in. And when we played in New York, half of those six violin players were contractors you know, one would hire the other. So they saw me playing in the band, so when I quit — when the band folded really — I went to New York and the rock & roll thing started hitting. See they were using a lot of different guitar players as opposed to only one, which was the case with the dance bands. So now they needed three guitar players, and they would say well they knew me, so get Bucky. So I was hired to play a lot of recordings because I knew the contractors. Maybe some better players came to town, but nobody knew who they were.
So you met the right people at the right time.
Yeah, at the right time
So you got in on doing some recording of the early rock & roll?
Yeah.
What did those charts look like at the time? Were they chord charts?

They were mostly rhythmic patterns. One guy playing a tight afterbeat, another guy playing [scats], you know those things, and another guy with a vibrolo [scats]. And after a while you say to yourself we could do that without the music, or fake the bass line with doubling the bass line with what they call a stop sound [scats]. You put your wrist on the strings and have a muffled sound. And that’s what I used to do.
Just that little lick that you were singing reminds me of a Paul Anka song. You did those things. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
Oh yeah, we made a lot of those. I made all records. The first six records with Dion and the Belmonts I had Mundell Lowe was on guitar, George Barnes, all jazz guys on those rock & roll records.
I didn’t realize that.

Yeah. Billy Bauer from the Woody Herman band, Osie Johnson, Panama Francis played drums, and none of us had those exotic guitars they use, that you see on these videos today. We had old fashioned archtop guitars with little Diamond pick-ups on them.
It’s interesting when you listen to some of the early — especially the Chuck Berry records — that he was into the straight eighth note rock & roll thing.
Oh yeah.
But the rhythm section was kind of still playing a swing mode.
That’s right.
Like they’re feeling each other, like what’s going on here now.

Well we were on a session, I’ll never forget, I know it was Tony Mottola playing guitar and Sol Gubin was playing drums, and a couple of other guitar players. And it was Paul Simon, believe me. And he kept saying I don’t like what I’m hearing from the guitars. And he picked up one of our guitars and played these eighth notes like you described, and that’s the feel he wanted, but none of us knew how to do it. But he had that in his mind way back when he first started. I don’t think these records ever came out but they might be in the can yet at MGM.
Yeah he actually had his first duo, it was called Tom and Jerry I think, and he didn’t really make it at that point, maybe that’s what you were talking about.

I actually played with him once, I had forgotten, I had played with so many different people that I had made a record with him and he was a guest on The Tonight Show with Garfunkel. I got a call, I was home, and they said we need a bass guitar and you’re the one that made the record or something. So I had to race in play that one number with them.
On bass?
On the bass guitar, but it was a six string bass guitar. It was an octave lower than the regular guitar, and it doubled the string bass.
Wow. I love listening to the difference in the way they recorded things back then too, in that the bass wasn’t nearly as prominent as in pop music nowadays.
Oh yeah. It finally got to that Fender bass and it got too loud, I mean for me, I never liked that.
Well how did the — you got on the NBC staff?
Yeah, well I was on about three different times on NBC. I mean when I left Vaughn Monroe I went right on NBC with the Kate Smith Show. And that was live, five days a © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
week. That’s how I got the job, the cello player knew there was an opening, Brownie his name was, Maurice Brown, and he says, “Go over and see Roy Shields, he’s looking for a guitar player.”
Was this radio you’re talking about?
No television.
A live T.V. show.
And I went up and he said, “Yeah we need a guitar player, you start Tuesday.” So I went up and played and I was making $250 a week. It was a lot of money.
Just for that show.

Just for that show but you had to do five days a week. And it was so, in those days, if you were on staff, other than doing the Kate Smith Show, maybe you’d only do two or three days a week so you’d make the same money.
And so you’d have a short rehearsal before the show.
We’d rehearse in the morning at eleven and we were out of there by five or six in the evening.
So you could play at night too?

I did. In fact one of the guests in one of the groups was the Three Suns. They were playing a block away at the Astor Hotel. That consisted of organ, guitar and accordion. They had a very big hit called “The Peg O My Heart,” and “Twilight Time.” They wrote the song, a very big song.
Didn’t someone record that with words later on?

The Platters, yeah. But they came on it and I had known them because they were guests on the Vaughn Monroe Show. And unfortunately the guitar player was unable to play, Al Nevins, and I jumped in and subbed for him. I put on his gray tuxedo and played on his D’Angelico guitar which I still have. And in the evening they asked me to play at the Astor Hotel — everything was a block away. I lived two blocks away at The Woodby on 45th Street. Kate Smith was on 44th Street and the Astor was between us.
You just walked to all these gigs.

Yeah. I could walk and everything. And when Kate Smith’s show ended that season I went to — I joined the group as a regular. And Al stayed in New York and hooked up with Donny — I can’t think of his last name off hand — but he became a big publisher.
This was ‘56?
‘54. ‘54 and ‘55. And he became a very big publisher. He had like 45 writers coming — Carole King, people like that.
Oh, and the Brill Building.
Not the Brill, the other one, 1650 Broadway.
Yeah they just churned out those tunes. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

And all Al would do is pick up the phone and call Connie Francis or somebody, “Hey we need a tenth song for the album.” Boom they shoot down and they had demos made. They made them down in the cellar of the same building, churn them out. Neil Sedaka was one of the writers too. They all became very, very big you know.
So if you were to listen, to sit and listen to the oldies radio station — oldies meaning ‘50s and ‘60s music — you’re likely to hear yourself now and then, right?

“Stand By Me” I made and I never realized until they sent me a check because they used the record in a movie, and somehow my son said, “Did you make this record.” I said, “I don’t remember this.” Because we did it three times a day. We were at all the major companies, 10-1 in the morning, 2-5, 7-10 at night, and sometimes a midnight session.
Amazing.
Yup.
There was a core of people that were — what do they call it — first call?
Yeah.
Like Milt Hinton.

Milt was there all the time. Milt and George Duvivier. I mean we had all jazz people. I mean the drummers were all from that, from the big bands, all from the big bands. And then once they got that eighth note feel, they were in.
That’s really interesting.
And the tenor players all had to play those chicken solos — that’s what they called them.
The chicken solos.
And King Curtis was the champ, and Sam the Man Taylor.
How did you guys feel about this music?

Well we were making money you know, and we could play gigs at night, but we got so busy we had no time to play gigs, no time. But I used to do, on Fridays and Saturdays, I played over in Jersey with a trio — piano, bass and guitar — all the time. I always had a little thing like that going on the side.
Keep your jazz chops.

Well not to keep them but I just did it automatically because I felt that this is what I like to do so I’ll make some money and support the family and everything doing the recordings, and go play for — I don’t know it was $35 or $40 a night to play that kind of music.
Keeps things in perspective I suppose. And you had a family by this time.

Oh yeah. We were all grown up and I tried to make it work you know, but then in the middle of that whole thing I got hooked up with Benny Goodman you know. And that changed everything around. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
I think that’s great because you mentioned when you were just learning the guitar that your uncles said, “Now listen to this Benny Goodman record.”
Oh definitely, oh yeah.
And then you end up playing with him.

Oh that’s a big thrill too. I always think of that. And I always also think when I was in high school on our own time we had an orchestra. And I played the bass in the orchestra, because they had no guitar parts, but if they needed a guitar I could play it. But we had violins, we might have had 14 violins playing. Every morning it would be a half hour before we started class we were rehearsing. And maybe an hour after school in the afternoon we were rehearsing again. And I always had the sound of those violins in my ear. So when Vaughn Monroe had those violins playing I said I heard this before. And some of the other guys never played with violins, I mean older guys. So that’s an advantage. When you learn something, you get a sound in your early days, you can only enhance that. It’s in your favor.
There was something I wanted to ask you about the studio scene that you were so much a part of. What was the racial make-up of the studio musicians at that time?

Oh there were a lot of blacks and all mixed in. In fact all the rhythm sections were that, and they had horn players, and before we got out of the business we had a violin section. But nobody knew who was playing because half the time they wouldn’t put your name on the record. But if you wanted a good feel, you had a great mixture of different people.
You had four children?
Yeah.
They were pretty musical?
Yeah every one of them play something.
We’ll talk about John in a while. The Tonight Show orchestra. How did that come about?

Well because I was up to here with the rock & roll and I felt it slipping away because those old licks that I knew so well weren’t being used anymore, and there were new sounds coming in that I wasn’t even ready to even try to do it. And I heard some new kids coming up and playing some great solos, and I says let me get out of here.
When you say “new sounds,” was it partly new technology? New amps?

Well it was. It was the feel of the records changed. But you know when you listen to those old ‘50s rock & roll records, that’s got to be one of the greatest rhythm feels ever. I mean if you want to call it jazz it’s still got that feel. It was airtight, and you couldn’t make the record unless every beat was right there, the way they locked it in. And then it became very loose, it became folkish or whatever.
Less arranged almost. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Yeah. And then the set groups were playing now. They weren’t using studio guys. Record companies turned over the studios to a group. Now the group would sit around all day long trying to make a track. A rhythm track. And nobody could get in — Mitch Miller couldn’t get into his own studios down there because some group was sitting there trying to make rhythm tracks, and they’re subtracting and adding — take this out, put this in— waste of time. Big waste of time and money. So I didn’t want to get in on that so Gene Bertoncini quit the show and they asked me to do it with Skitch Henderson, and that was one of the best moves I ever made. Because I played better music and we were featured a lot, playing the kind of music that I knew how to play. Well Doc Severinsen was in the band, Bob Haggart played the bass, Hymie Schertzer, who played lead alto with Benny Goodman. I mean it was the best in the world. And I’m sitting there with Al Klink who played with Glenn Miller, and Clark Terry, Maxwell, Jimmy Maxwell, Snooky Young. I mean that band was incredible.
And what was the schedule like for that show?

We did five days a week, but I used to split that up with Tony Mottola who was on staff. He’d do two nights, I’d do three nights. And if we had a recording I would sub for him, I would go in and do his night and then he’d make it up another time.
Do you remember any funny or weird instance of The Tonight Show orchestra with people coming on that you had to back up?

Well you know that show was great, the band was great because we had everybody played whatever they felt when they were asked to do it. So if somebody came on and Skitch would go into something, we never rehearsed. Skitch never rehearsed. We had music up there and the only time we’d play is when they were off the air, we played for the audience and then you might hear a little of the band. But we were forever just getting there on time from another session just in time to play the theme.
No kidding. What a life, huh? You recorded some marvelous duo records, in fact I think you said some of your best things are duos?

Oh yeah. My favorite records are — the first duo I made was with Tony Mottola, then I got hooked up with George Barnes who is one of America’s great individual guitar players I ever heard, nobody played like George, and he was in the studio scene with us. And he was fed up with them, so he always had little projects going on with jazz on the weekend somewhere, and some little project where he arranged something that had a lot of body to it, and Jack Lesberg was involved, I was, George, and then George and I really hooked up when I got my seven string guitar. Because he had been playing duets with Carl Kress, one of my heroes.
And Zoot Sims and Stephane Grappelli, all those folks.
Oh, yeah. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
When you got together to do a duo record with some of those people, mostly just talking through tunes, picking out tunes, did you rehearse it a lot?

Well at first I would say with Tony Mottola, Tony took advantage of the seven string and we made a couple of beautiful records together because Tony was a very lyrical player. And then the same with George Barnes, and it was a different approach. George and I went through a fake book one night out in Jersey with the machine, the recording machine on, we played one tune after another, like just turned page after page. Go into it, play it, and we had, oh we had enough for about ten albums. But it was the beginning of the duet. And we finally honed it down and we made a couple of great albums, because we were playing in the evenings. I was playing at the St. Regis. After the Tonight Show I’d go over there and play with George. And we got some good notices and we made an album, we made two albums. We made one live at the Town Hall with McLaughlin, Charlie Byrd.
John McLaughlin? Charlie Byrd?

Yeah, he was on the bill. Tiny Grimes, the famous Tiny Grimes with the four string guitar who played with Art Tatum. Joe Beck, Chuck Wayne. All the same place. But we knew what we were doing. They were — you know who else was there? Benson. And they were all rehearsing in a corner with Major Holley and a drummer, you know, I want to do this, I want to do that, and I’m saying boy, it’s too late for that. Well that’s the way the business is you know, but we had set groups and we went out there and we played — when they released the album we had one side of an LP all to ourselves from the company to do what we did.
I’m curious, when you’re working with two guitars like that, and you are going to be doing some substitution chords or something like that, how do you communicate that with your partner?

You just lay it in there and all of a sudden, George heard it, bang, he went right with it. That was the beauty of two guitars. It’s communication more than preparing. We knew, we perceived what the other was doing all the time. And I’ll tell you, with George Barnes, sparks used to fly when he was on. Whew. I mean he used to go into high gear once in a while, I mean I wish I had a tape machine. I mean I remember it all here. So I mean when somebody tells me that somebody else is a great guitar player, I says you better watch out because I worked with George Barnes.
Yeah. It makes you play that much better too, right?
Oh of course. It puts you, it lifts you right up. And sometimes we got serious and we got together and you do this and you do that, look out, it got fierce.
So you’ve never worked a non-music job in your life, is that right?
That’s true, yeah. Never. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
That’s saying something.
That’s 53 years of playing the guitar.
Well I have something I wanted to play for you.
[audio interlude]
It’s George.
Listen.
Oh that’s John [Pizzarelli Junior]. Well he got that from George.
He got that from George? This is wild. That was great how it came out of that.
It’s George’s arrangement.
Yeah?
Yeah. We got that from George. In fact we sent his widow a copy of this.
Marvelous.
Yeah, Evelyn.
It almost sounds like you guys had played some banjo along the way too.
Well that’s what it’s from. You know John studied banjo with my uncles, and they had this wrist thing going, so you apply it to guitar, that’s what happens.
And John plays seven string also?
Oh yeah. He played seven string right away.
He’s been getting some great press.
Yeah.
It’s great — the Pizzarelli name is out there.

Yeah we’re going to — I haven’t played with him that much but when we do we do right into it. We can get that thing going right away. But we’re going to play at the Smithsonian in November. There’s an archtop exhibition going on, all the best guitar makers have made blue guitars.
No kidding.

And Scott Shinnery from New Jersey owns them all. He commissioned them all and they’re doing a thing in the Smithsonian. We’re going to do our own thing, and then maybe play a couple of acoustic duets on the blue guitars.
What’s it going to be called? Does it have a name for the exhibition?
No, I don’t know. It’s at the Smithsonian.
You guys probably, I’m trying to think what his attitude would have been to his father when he was coming up. Did he get into some rock bands?
Oh he had that way before he started playing a seven string. He’s got a stack of songs he wrote. They’re all over the house — lyrics and chord symbols, and wa wa pedals.
Was he influenced by what, The Beatles, or even more recent people? © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

I don’t know, everybody. Chick Corea — I think he liked Chick Corea right away. In fact that’s how I learned “Spain,” I heard them playing and I says gee I played that on the classical guitar. That’s where it’s from Concierto de Aranjuez by Rodrigo.
What was his attitude toward what you do? Did he realize how much playing you had done up to that point?

Well he knew, but I think it set in when we played one summer together at the Pierre Hotel. I was playing there with a trio and in the summer they cut down and said can you just come in with two guitars and make it easy? And John did it with me and then he got his baptism of fire there with me giving him the dirty looks when he hit the wrong chord. And he gave them to me when I did. But fortunately he can sit down with a tune and come up with a good set of chords for it. That’s what I like about him.
Good singer too.
Yeah. Well he heard all the — he heard Nat King Cole and Joe Mooney from Paterson, New Jersey, who is the father of all the right chords for my money.
You’ve had quite an on and off association with Stephane Grappelli.

Yeah. That was something I never planned on, it was the same as going with Benny Goodman. You say to yourself wow, here I am with Benny. I played with Benny a long time and then to add to that, I was called to go with Stephane at the Boston Pops, just a duet, honoring Joe Venuti, who I had played with until he died. And we did a couple of Joe’s tunes, “I’ll Never be the Same” and a couple of tunes that he made famous with Eddie Lang. Then our association began because when Stephane came to the United States he preferred to have an American bass player and an American guitarist. He left his group back home. And it gave him a different outlook, instead of playing the same old stuff all the time. So we had to do what he wanted, and we tried our best to do it.
Speaking of Joe Venuti, were you ever on the receiving end of any of his practical jokes?

I’ve seen situations that it got into, in fact everything carried right to his funeral. I went down and played his funeral and there might have been three or four violin players from Philadelphia, all arguing about how he played the ending of a certain tune that they wanted to play for the service. I said Joe must be laughing you know.
He pulled some good stunts along the way.
Oh yeah.
I guess a sense of humor helps in the jazz world.

Well he was a tough guy you know. He said you couldn’t quit his band, he’d beat you up. And then when he got sick and tired of the band he had, because they were traveling with cars, he would go around and put signs in different directions so that when the guys followed the signs to certain places, half of the band went one way and the other half went the other way. That’s the only way he could break the band up. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

That was his way of giving notice, huh? He sent you out in the sticks somewhere. That’s good. I had mentioned I read something in Milt Hinton’s book about one of the greatest gigs that he ever played he felt was with you and Bob Rosengarden and Benny Goodman at the Rainbow Room I think it was?
Oh yeah.
With John Bunch.
Yeah. We played, I remember we played about three weeks, three or four weeks. And it was a great rhythm section. And Benny played of course and I think Urbie Green was there, was Urbie on that too?
I think he did mention that.

And then Lionel Hampton sat in, oh Peter Appleyard played vibes, and one night Lionel came in and sat in with us. And Johnny Mercer came up and sang with us one night. So things like that were happening a lot.
And these days, you split your time between going around to these jazz parties and doing recording. Have you got a recording session planned coming up?

No the only records we make now for companies that want to make a jazz record like Arbors or the company I used to be with, LRC Records with New York Swing, it’s John Bunch and Jay Leonhart, just a trio, and then we add drums, either Bernard Purdie or Dennis Mackrel or Joe Cocuzzo. But we found out that it works better on the road with just three, without the drums.
That’s a fairly popular combination.

Well Nat Cole put it together, and everybody used it. Art Tatum had the same thing and I mean he did it because they get more money as opposed to playing solo piano. They told him put Tiny Grimes in and Slam Stewart and according to Tiny, he never told him what tune he was playing. They were just there and Art’s making big money and never said anything. In fact the funny line was that Tiny said, “It was a great honor but it really wasn’t a great pleasure,” or something like that.
Yeah? He didn’t even tell them what tune he was going to play.
Well he just got up on the stage and started playing.
I’ve always wondered what that would have been like to try to keep up with Art Tatum.

Well I don’t know. Listen to the records. I know, but Slam could. Slam had that uncanny knack of whatever was going on, I don’t care what, if you’re tapping on a tin can, he could make it work. I think he was the greatest bass player ever. The greatest bow soloist I ever heard on the bass I mean he had such a beat in his playing, and his control of that violin. He had the same control of his bow as Heifitz did on the violin. I mean that’s the weapon when you want to evaluate a good violin player, it’s how he holds the bow and what control he has on it, not what he does. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
I want to take you back a moment. Something you were talking about, music education. You seemed to say that the musicians were over educated these days.

Yes. Over trained. Well everybody goes in school and they want to be a soloist today. So they go and they learn how to read and they do ensemble playing and they learn to read so well that when they get with a band, a commercial band, it’s boring. They could play it, like I said before, without even thinking about it. So when boredom sets in on any musician, you better quit the business. You’ve got to like what you’re doing. And I think the big thing with the dance bands, half of those guys, and I mean this as a compliment, couldn’t read well, but they could feel the music. And I know, without mentioning any names, the best guys would sit there and learn the parts and in a week or so they’d have the whole book down. Plus when they had to play these four measure solos and eight measure solos, they were gems. I mean they used to write those solos out in Down Beat you know, so-and-so’s solo here, he played this on it, and you’d analyze that and it was incredible.
Yeah. Instant classic.

Oh Billy Butterfield, a great example, all those Artie Shaw solos, all Benny’s, Lou McGarrity and Vido Musso on “Jersey Bounce,” and the guy that played, I think it was Rollini, on “Stomping at the Savoy.” I mean they were great solos.
And it wasn’t just a matter of playing as many notes as they could in the time they had?
No. They were swinging. Swinging all the time. If they weren’t, Benny wouldn’t have them.
He’d give them that look?
Well, the look, you know. The look was nothing. The look was an afterthought. Benny would do that.
The opinions you get about him seem to be very different. Some people felt that he went out of his way to be nasty to them, and other people felt that he just was — that the music was —

That was his way of telling you he wanted something. He wanted the beat. He wanted to get the kick in the pants from you. And if you didn’t get it, he would harass you a little bit. I know I worked with Sonny Igoe who played with Benny a long time, maybe one of his last great bands, you know. It might have been the bebop band he had. That Benny looked at him, you know, gave him the bit, and looked at him straight in the eye, and Sonny went like this. And Benny never bothered him anymore. And Benny always used to like look at the set up and say “uh, drums, move a little bit this way.” No matter what. And Grady Tate used to go BANG and hit a big hard rim shot. And then he’d say “leave the drums there.”
Enough said. That’s good. Oh boy. What’s in the future for you, coming up? © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

Well next week I’m playing with Rosemary Clooney, two weeks at the Rainbow Room. And I’m doing a concert with John. I’m doing a couple of symphony dates with Skitch Henderson in Florida, in Tampa, four dates — Clearwater, St. Petersburg, Tampa. I get a big kick out of doing that too. I’m playing things that I used to listen to on record, a score by Victor Young called “For Whom The Bell Tolls.” It’s something that we all used to listen to when we were young: listen to this — and listen to this. And the record was worn out in one spot. And 40 years later I’m playing the same tune.
That’s marvelous.
So you know it’s a big kick. And it’s something I didn’t push, but there I am. I did it three weeks ago with Skitch at Carnegie Hall.
Man you have been around.
Yeah.
You played at the White House a number of times?
I played there twice. Once with Benny Goodman and Buddy Rich and Milt Hinton, Hank Jones.
Good company.
And the second time was with Sinatra, with just a small group. Tony Mottola, myself.
Do you and your son handle business in a different way? Has the business of music changed?

Well he’s on a different plateau. John gets big money with his group. So I mean they go to Brazil and there’s the bookers, and there’s enough money. And they draw. That’s the secret. If you ask a guy for a lot of money and you get there and there’s 20 people sitting in the audience, you better give that money back. You have to.
You have to give it back?

Well I’m saying to myself, you didn’t draw. You didn’t draw the people. So even on the small jobs I do, I count heads all the time. When I was at The Pierre Hotel, I knew how much it cost each person to get in there, whatever it was, it was on your tab. And I knew I was making money for them. It reminds me of a funny story of Benny doing a gig down south. He got there and somehow everything was loused up. They changed the venue, they had the wrong date in the paper, everything was wrong. So when he got there the promoter said, “Here’s your money” whatever it was, seven grand in those days. And he says — it was a total bust, there was eleven people in the audience. And Benny says, “Never mind, we’re going to play anyway.” He played the whole gig, and when it was over Benny said, “Guys, that’s the best I ever played.”
Those eleven people got the show of their life.
But he was like that.
He was very professional. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
Oh yeah. He took care of business. But if somebody at the other end louses it up for you, and it’s out of control.
Well I enjoyed listening to you last night in good company here in Aspen and I was struck by your attack on the guitar. You have a very strong attack.
Well I feel like that. You know when I play with Ross Tompkins and — who is the other piano player who played last night?
Ralph Sutton and Dave McKenna.

And Dave. I haven’t played with Dave, I haven’t seen him in a couple of years. You get up there and you just forget, and you say wow, something different is happening. You know just sitting there floating. And I can hear him here and I hear what’s going on and with Peplowski, bringing everything down. And it makes you play better. And that’s where I get my — I don’t know I start hitting the guitar a different way. You do that. But if you’re all on the level up there, you can’t go anywhere. And I like to play up and down, no matter what kind of tune it is. If it’s a fast song it’s got to be here sometimes, it’s got to get down, it’s got to be up.
Yeah. You have to give the listener some levels to —
That’s right. You have to build. You have to start with nothing, get up to something, then come down to nothing. And sometimes less is better.
Those are good words. We’ll put those in capitals.

No it is true. The same with an arrangement. If you’ve going to write an arrangement and all of a sudden the singer sings something, and you’ve got the whole band coming in, there’s no place for it to go. You’ve got to let the rhythm play first. Like Count Basie, there is the best example. They start —
Chunk, chunk, chunk.

And maybe 32 measures later you hear: waaaaaa, and it knocks you right out of your seat. That’s good music. MR. In a sense it has similarity to classical music. You know when you play tapes in your car for instance, if you play rock & roll, you can usually set it at one volume and hear it. With classical music sometimes it gets so low that you can’t hear it.

That’s right. But it works with an arrangement. And when you look at a score and you see notes and notes and notes where one phrase ends and you see another section picking it up, I can tell a good arrangement as soon as I look at the guitar part. But then I don’t know what’s going on, and the only way I can help that arrangement, if you’re involved with it, take away. Say don’t have the violins come in until say 16 measures. And then all of a sudden you get different colors coming in and then you come right down to where you were. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
That reminds me of some stories I’ve heard about Basie. When arrangers would come in with their thing and he’d say, “Well this is good but—”
Well “Li’l Darlin’” was fast, and they played and Basie suggested playing it real slow, one-two-three-four. Biggest hit they ever had. Neal Hefti wrote it.
Can you imagine Neal Hefti going, now what are you doing? That slow?
Well if you think about it he didn’t interfere with one note on that, or a chord or anything. He just said play it slower. I mean does that work?
I guess that was his genius right there.

Of course. Oh Basie was a master. Well Basie played with Benny you know on a couple of records. “Airmail Special” I think he’s on one of those records. MR. Do you have any advice for those over educated young musicians coming out of school these days?

Well I mean utilize the education you got, which we never got. We learned hard knocks you know. Somebody’d say you’re playing the wrong chord or do this or do that. Sometimes it’s costly. You’re on a job and you don’t get the job back. But you have to learn the repertoire. The repertoire is Jerome Kern, Johnny Mercer, Duke Ellington, Richard Rogers, Cole Porter, Walter Donaldson, people like that, Harry Warren. And it takes about this much space on your shelf. And for about five bucks a piece, or seven dollars maybe now, you can buy everybody’s book. That’s where it’s all at, right in there. All the changes. Learn the song the way the guy wrote it first. And then apply all that slick stuff you learned in school and sometime you’re going to end up playing exactly the way it’s written.
After all is said and done?

That’s right. Well Dave McKenna, best example, how a song should be harmonized. And the hardest thing, harder than writing an arrangement, is to write a set of chords for an arrangement. Say you only have four people in the band. And now all you need is the right chord and the right bass note. Bobby Scott told me that years ago. He said, “Over night, I sat up all night trying to figure out where you wanted the bass to go.” And you’ve got to look underneath the song itself and say hey, there’s a lot of beauty here, let’s make it happen.
Well I like those words, especially at 9:50 in the morning. Terrific sentiments.

No but if you want to hear great arrangements, listen to anything Johnny Mandel wrote or Robert Farnon who was the daddy of all the arrangers. He’s got some great albums, Schwartz and Dietz songs, made in England, unbelievable orchestrations.
A recent Joe Williams record he did.

Oh yeah that’s right, he did Joe’s last album. But I mean he did an instrumental and then you hear the melody with either violin or trombone or maybe electric guitar playing like © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

George Shearing and his little ensemble with vibes, but what’s going on behind them is unbelievable. All correct. All correct. And then if you’re an English literature major, buy a book on Richard Rogers’ songs and it’s all in there.
All the words.
All the words. Without the music.
I guess that’s mark of a great lyric. If you take the music away you still have a —
Of course. Schwartz and Dietz, all those songs, “I guess I’ll have to change my plan” and all that stuff. It makes a lot of sense.
By the way you play on one of my new favorite albums, and that is Dick Hyman “The Age of Swing.”
Oh yeah, I like that concept because it has a Count Basie flair to it and that was the whole idea. We did it in New York State.
Purchase was it?
Purchase, New York.
Yeah. Just the sound of the recording.
Oh it was done on a stage in an empty theatre, and everything was natural.
Very nice.
Oh I enjoyed that. Yeah we made two of those. What’s the name of that company? Alliance?
Reference Recordings. Excellent. Well I want to thank you for your time today.
Oh you’re quite welcome. We could sit here all day, couldn’t we?
We could. We’ll probably have to do Part Two next time around.
Let’s do that.
We will. Next time we’re at another festival we’ll do it. Between then and now though, I want you to write down every recording you ever played on. Okay?
You know it’s something I couldn’t do.
I know. I asked Milt Hinton about that too and there are just hundreds and hundreds, right?
You know it’s the ones that my name doesn’t appear. We made so many records that nobody knows who’s playing what.
Do you suppose that’s written down anywhere?
Well only on the recording itself, on the contractor’s list of musicians on a certain date, where they were supposed to put the title of the song on the contract.
It would be some archival project for somebody, to try to straighten all that out some day.
My last recording session was with Tony Bennett, taking off Billie Holiday from the Basie band on a old soundie, and me playing along with her, playing rhythm with the © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
New York rhythm section, and they extracted her from the soundie and put her on our track, and then they took her off and made Tony sing a few lines.
Wow. Studio magic, huh?

Yeah. Phil Ramone. He’s one of the great engineers in the country, did that. In fact I think they made it longer, but it only ran a minute and twenty-six seconds from the soundie. But I was very happy about that. But they didn’t put our name on the record, nobody’s name.
Unsung heroes. Well you’ve had a great career and I’m sure it’s got many, many years to go.
Well thank you. I’m looking forward to keep on playing. Nothing else I know how to do.
Thanks for joining us today.
Okay. Thank you very much. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

segments.chapter: Opening and the seven-string guitar
segments.title: Archive copyright statement and biographical note
segments.summary: Boilerplate and an introductory note on Pizzarelli and the Jerome Jazz Party interview.

segments.chapter: Opening and the seven-string guitar
segments.title: Playing a seven-string guitar after George Van Eps
segments.summary: Pizzarelli explains getting a seven-string Gretsch after hearing Van Eps, and other extra-string and tuning variations.

segments.chapter: Family and early years
segments.title: Uncles who taught him guitar and told him who to hear
segments.summary: Two uncles, a banjoist and a dance-band rhythm guitarist, taught him and steered his listening to Goodman, Van Eps and Charlie Christian.

segments.chapter: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
segments.title: Joining Vaughn Monroe at 17 before the draft
segments.summary: He joined Monroe in 1943, was drafted in April 1944, and got his job back after two years of service.

segments.chapter: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
segments.title: Army service in Manila and listening to V-discs
segments.summary: He did little but play basketball and music in Manila, and heard Nat King Cole and big bands on V-discs.

segments.chapter: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
segments.title: Monroe band dance jobs, bus tours and pay
segments.summary: Monroe's band had a jazz flair, arranger Johnny Watson and altoist Andy Bagni, and played dance jobs on long bus trips. He earned $125 a week plus $60 for the Camel Caravan radio show.

segments.chapter: Vaughn Monroe band and the army
segments.title: Today's over-trained players versus eight-bar solos then
segments.summary: Degrees in performance leave young players bored; swing-era soloists had to say something in eight bars.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Breaking into New York recording through violin contractors
segments.summary: After Monroe's band folded he got studio calls from contractors who knew him, as rock and roll needed several guitars; he describes the rhythm parts.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Early rock and roll sessions with jazz guitarists
segments.summary: He played on Dion and the Belmonts records alongside Mundell Lowe, George Barnes and others, and discusses the swing feel in early rock.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Paul Simon's session and playing bass guitar on The Tonight Show
segments.summary: Simon wanted straight eighth notes the guitarists could not play; later Pizzarelli played six-string bass for Simon and Garfunkel.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Kate Smith Show on NBC television
segments.summary: He joined the Kate Smith show on Maurice Brown's tip, earning $250 a week with a short daily rehearsal.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Subbing for Al Nevins with the Three Suns
segments.summary: He subbed for guitarist Al Nevins, then joined the Three Suns, while Nevins became a publisher at 1650 Broadway.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Publishing-house songwriters and recording "Stand By Me"
segments.summary: Nevins' publishing house churned out songs for Connie Francis; Pizzarelli did three sessions a day and forgot playing on "Stand By Me".

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: The first-call studio rhythm sections and chicken solos
segments.summary: Hinton and Duvivier plus big-band drummers formed the core, and tenor players like King Curtis played chicken solos.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Studio money, jazz gigs on the side, and meeting Goodman
segments.summary: Studio work paid well, he played weekend trio jobs in Jersey for $35-40, and Goodman then changed everything.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Goodman as a boyhood hero and the high school violins
segments.summary: Playing with Goodman was a thrill; his school orchestra's violins prepared him for Monroe's string section.

segments.chapter: New York studio and TV work
segments.title: Racial mix of studio musicians; his four children
segments.summary: Studio rhythm sections were mixed and often uncredited; he mentions his four musical children.

segments.chapter: Tonight Show and duo recordings
segments.title: Leaving rock and roll sessions for The Tonight Show band
segments.summary: He quit rock sessions as the sound changed and groups took over studios, and took Gene Bertoncini's place in Skitch Henderson's band.

segments.chapter: Tonight Show and duo recordings
segments.title: Tonight Show schedule and playing without rehearsal
segments.summary: He split the week with Tony Mottola; Skitch never rehearsed and players arrived from other sessions just in time for the theme.

segments.chapter: Tonight Show and duo recordings
segments.title: Duo records with Mottola and George Barnes
segments.summary: His favorite records are duos, starting with Mottola, then George Barnes after he got the seven-string.

segments.chapter: Tonight Show and duo recordings
segments.title: Duo albums with Barnes and the Town Hall guitar concert
segments.summary: He and Barnes recorded from a fake book, played the St. Regis, and made a live Town Hall album with other guitarists on the bill.

segments.chapter: Tonight Show and duo recordings
segments.title: Communication between two guitars and never working a non-music job
segments.summary: Two guitarists communicate by perception rather than preparation; Pizzarelli praises Barnes and says he never had a non-music job.

segments.chapter: John Pizzarelli and Grappelli
segments.title: Hearing John play George Barnes's arrangement
segments.summary: Rowe plays a recording in which John Pizzarelli uses Barnes's arrangement and a banjo-derived wrist technique learned from the uncles.

segments.chapter: John Pizzarelli and Grappelli
segments.title: John Pizzarelli's career and playing with him at the Pierre
segments.summary: His son John plays seven-string, upcoming Smithsonian blue-guitar exhibition, John's influences, and their summer at the Pierre Hotel.

segments.chapter: John Pizzarelli and Grappelli
segments.title: Working with Stephane Grappelli after the Venuti tribute
segments.summary: He was called for a Boston Pops duet honoring Venuti, which began his association with Grappelli.

segments.chapter: John Pizzarelli and Grappelli
segments.title: Joe Venuti's funeral and pranks on his band
segments.summary: Anecdotes about Venuti: violinists arguing at his funeral and signs that split his band on the road.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: A Rainbow Room engagement with Benny Goodman
segments.summary: The Rainbow Room weeks with Goodman, John Bunch and others, with Hampton and Mercer sitting in.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Current recording and the New York Swing trio
segments.summary: He records for Arbors and LRC with John Bunch and Jay Leonhart's trio, preferring three players on the road.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Art Tatum's trio, Tiny Grimes and Slam Stewart
segments.summary: Tatum's trio format, Tiny Grimes's remark, and praise for Slam Stewart's bow control.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Dance-band musicians who felt the music and short solos
segments.summary: Dance-band players often could not read well but played gem solos; examples from Shaw and Goodman, and Goodman's swing.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Goodman's look and the drummers
segments.summary: Goodman's stare was his way of asking for the beat; stories about Sonny Igoe and Grady Tate.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Upcoming dates with Clooney and Henderson, and White House performances
segments.summary: His coming engagements, Victor Young's score played 40 years on, and two White House performances.

segments.chapter: Benny Goodman, Basie and the swing era
segments.title: Counting heads and Goodman's gig with eleven people
segments.summary: Pizzarelli compares John's draw with his own and tells of Goodman playing a full gig to eleven people.

segments.chapter: Education, advice and arranging
segments.title: Strong attack, playing with pianists, and building dynamics
segments.summary: Playing with Sutton, McKenna and Peplowski changes his attack, and he explains building a performance from nothing up.

segments.chapter: Education, advice and arranging
segments.title: Count Basie, "Li'l Darlin'" and writing arrangements
segments.summary: On arrangements that leave room, Basie slowing down "Li'l Darlin'", and Basie recording with Goodman.

segments.chapter: Education, advice and arranging
segments.title: Advice to young musicians: learn the standard repertoire
segments.summary: Learn the standards as written, then apply school tricks; Dave McKenna and chord writing for small groups.

segments.chapter: Education, advice and arranging
segments.title: Favorite arrangers and the value of lyrics
segments.summary: Praise for Johnny Mandel and Robert Farnon, and Rodgers and Schwartz and Dietz lyrics.

segments.chapter: Education, advice and arranging
segments.title: Dick Hyman's The Age of Swing recording
segments.summary: He recorded the album in an empty theatre at Purchase, New York, with a Basie flair.

segments.chapter: Closing
segments.title: Wrapping up and the impossibility of listing all his recordings
segments.summary: Thanks, plans for a second part, and the uncredited sessions he cannot list.

segments.chapter: Closing
segments.title: Last session with Tony Bennett and goodbyes
segments.summary: His latest session made Billie Holiday and Tony Bennett share a track, uncredited, then goodbyes.
